Similarly, end uses that are more flexible will be able to be operated at much lower average prices than those that cannot be flexed as much. Figure 19 shows the per-kWh cost of operating various end uses with and without price response, across 33 sectors, utilities, and tariff design scenarios. As with other figures, the 2030 low price forecast scenario is shown. Across all scenarios, residential cooling and level 2 EVs have the highest baseline effective rate, as shown by the top of the gray bars. This is because our baseline load model has these end uses operating primarily in the summer (in the case of cooling) and the evenings (in the case of EVs), which are the times of highest prices. Space heating and pool and spa pumps tend to have lower baseline operating costs. Sectoral differences are not particularly pronounced, even though large non-res customers typically pay much less per kWh than res customers, because small non-res customers have similar rates to the residential sector, bringing up the non-res sectors’ averages. The colored bars in Figure 19 show the cost of operating each end use after responding to the price. Therefore, the height of the gray bars represents the per-kWh savings possible from the load flexibility. Under a Full dynamic price tariff design, the savings potential for level 2 EVs is particularly dramatic, with per-kWh costs dropping to about 10% of their baseline values. Again, this is partly due to our baseline model assuming that customers, in the absence of price responsive behaviors, will be charging their cars in the evening when prices are very high. Because these loads are very flexible, they can take advantage of the lowest prices offered, with the average EV charging cost being less than 10 cents per kWh across all three utilities (in nominal 2030 dollars). Pool and spa pumps also see substantial savings, with per-kWh costs cut in half to under 30 cents per kWh across all utilities. Savings for space heating are the most limited, due to the more limited flexibility of the end use and the fact that they already operate at lower-price times, so the potential savings within a given flexibility window are limited. Looking at the Medium, and especially Mild, tariff designs show much more restricted savings across all end uses. EVs, for example, must pay closer to 30 and 40 cents per kWh on the Medium and Mild tariffs, respectively. On the Mild tariff, all end uses in all utilities pay at least 35 cents per kWh, except for crop irrigation in SCE territory. These per-kWh end use costs could have substantial impacts not only on the value of being price responsive, but on the likelihood of customers electrifying end uses to begin with.
